text.p: Brand-name companies are fighting a growing number of so-called "copy cat" products -- and sometimes suing over the issue -- but consumers love the cheaper, look-alike brands, experts said on Wednesday.
Industry experts told Reuters shoppers welcomed "copy cat" brands that are sold by supermarkets under the supermarket name but look similar to brand-name products.
"Consumers really rather approve of look-alike brands," says Roy Gundersen, a partner of Butcher Gundersen, a design consultancy which has carried out research with groups of shoppers.

"They compare supermarket 'own-label' products with famous brand names, think they look similar and believe they are of similar quality. They then make a decision based on price, because 'own label' is invariably cheaper," he said.
Look-alike brands are appearing more and more frequently on British supermarket shelves and include everything from breakfast cereals to soft drinks.
One packaging designer told Reuters he had been asked by a supermarket chain to design things that looked like famous brand name products.
"I declined -- but it does go on," he said.
His experience is unlikely to go down well with branded manufacturers for whom "copy cat" brands have become a legal issue.
United Biscuits food manufacturer is currently battling it out in the British High Court with Asda Group Plc , a British supermarket group.

A spokeswoman for United Biscuits told Reuters the company was suing Asda for trademark infringement. The case centres on Asda's Puffin brand of chocolate biscuits which United Biscuits says infringes the trademark of its Penguin chocolate biscuit.
Asda denies infringing United Biscuits' trademark and accused United Biscuit in a statement this week of unfairly trying to limit competition.
The price difference between brand-name products and those accused of copying them can be dramatic.
A pack of Puffins with 14 biscuits, for instance, which costs 99 pence ($1.62), is 25 percent cheaper than a similar pack of Penguins which costs 1.35 pounds.

Industry experts say they expect more supermarket own- brands to be the subject of court cases. "I don't think this is the last of it," said Kevin Vise, former packaging design manager for supermarket chain Tesco, who now researches consumer attitudes to brands.
Gundersen added, "I think if overt copy-cat brands increase then eventually restrictive legislation will be introduced either by the British government or by the EU (European Union)."
